The Second Temple Period, spanning from around five hundred sixteen BCE to seventy CE, refers to the era when a reconstructed temple stood on the Temple Mount in Jerusalem following the return of Jewish exiles from Babylon. This period witnessed the development of rabbinic Judaism, the flourishing of Jewish sectarian movements including Pharisees, Sadducees, and Essenes, and dramatic encounters with Hellenistic and Roman powers, culminating in the temple's destruction by Roman legions in seventy CE.

The Second Temple was constructed after the Babylonian Exile when Cyrus the Great permitted Jewish exiles to return to Judaea under Zerubbabel around five hundred sixteen BCE. The temple was extensively renovated and expanded by King Herod the Great, who ruled from thirty-seven to four BCE, making it one of the grandest religious structures of the ancient Mediterranean world.

During the Second Temple Period, Torah study and rabbinic interpretation displaced temple sacrifices as the center of Jewish religious practice, laying the groundwork for post-temple Rabbinic Judaism. Jewish sectarian movements emerged and competed for religious authority. The Pharisees emphasized oral law and resurrection. The Sadducees were priestly conservatives skeptical of resurrection and oral tradition. The Essenes formed ascetic communities.

The Maccabean Revolt occurred from one hundred sixty-seven to one hundred sixty BCE when the Seleucid king Antiochus IV desecrated the temple by dedicating it to Zeus. The Maccabees rededicated it, an event commemorated by Hanukkah. The temple was destroyed by Roman legions under the future emperor Titus in seventy CE during the First Jewish-Roman War. This event is mourned annually on Tisha B'Av. Only the Western Wall remained standing.
